html:
From the late 1860s to the First World War, a large share of Lithuanians emigrated, most of them to the United States. They fled poverty, famine and service in the Russian army.

Most settled in the coal towns of Pennsylvania and in Chicago, working in mines and stockyards. Upton Sinclair's novel The Jungle tells of a Lithuanian family in the Chicago meatpacking yards. Lithuanian newspapers printed in America were smuggled home during the press ban.

A second wave of refugees came after the Second World War, fleeing the Soviet return. The diaspora lobbied for Lithuania through the occupation. A new wave of emigration after 2004 sent many to Britain and Ireland. Compare Norwegian emigration.
